title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache (cost model)
summary: AE+SE walkthrough of Redwood Optimize focused on batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations for Atlas Financial's transactional scoring service. Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs, recommended batching profiles, cache hit strategies, demo of cost model spreadsheet, and next steps for pilot benchmarking and security docs.
next_steps: Redwood: share cost model spreadsheet and recommended batch config (Maya) - by 2026-05-04
Customer: provide 2 week sample of traffic profile + sample prompts (Carlos) - by 2026-05-01
Schedule pilot kickoff and benchmarking window (calendar invite) - Maya to propose timeslots
action_items: Maya Chen - Send ROI / cost model spreadsheet + demo recording - due 2026-05-04
Jon Park - prepare end-to-end benchmark plan (p95 latency, tokens/sec) and test harness repo link - due 2026-05-06
Carlos Rivera - export 2 weeks of production traffic (anonymized) and share S3 link - due 2026-05-01

transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone thanks for joining, um, happy to get into the Optimize walkthrough today. We have Jon and Leah from engineering on the call to go deep on batching and KV cache.
[00:12] Sarah Lee: Thanks Maya, excited. We're specifically looking at the transactional scoring pipeline, low latency, lots of short prompts, about ~120 tokens per request on average, and cost is a big concern.
[00:25] Jon Park (SE): Awesome, that's a common profile. Quick confirm: p95 latency target?
[00:30] Priya Nair: We're aiming for p95 under 250ms for online scoring.
[00:35] Jon Park (SE): Got it. For that profile we typically recommend short-burst batching with KV/prefix cache for any repeated prefixes — we'll show the cost model that contrasts pure hosted single-request vs batching with cache hit assumptions.
[00:48] Carlos Rivera: Do you support our VPC/private deployment? We have regs around customer data staying in our VPC.
[00:54] Maya Chen: Yes we do; Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem. For this pilot we can run on Dedicated or Private depending on your security requirements. Kevin, I know you were looking at KMS stuff —
[01:04] Kevin O'Neill (Security): Yeah we need to know encryption at rest, KMS integration and audit log retention, SOC2 scope.
[01:09] Leah Ortiz: We have a standard SOC 2 artifact pack and KMS integrations; we'll add the SOC2 checklist and KMS notes to the security doc we share.
[01:15] Sarah Lee: Great. Can we jump into the Optimize UI and the cost model?
[01:19] Maya Chen: Sure we'll share the screen — starting on the Optimize tab, top right is the workload profile section.
[01:26] [01:26] Jon Park (SE): So first principle: batching reduces per-token compute overhead up to a point, but increases tail latency if you wait too long to build a batch. For transactional scoring with 120 tokens/request and a p95 target of 250ms, we usually recommend target batch sizes in the 4-12 range with max latency hold at 30-75ms depending on your tolerance.
[01:45] Priya Nair: Wait so hold latency 75ms doesn't that blow our p95?
[01:49] Jon Park (SE): Not necessarily — hold latency is the extra queuing time to assemble batch. If your model per-token time is small and the GPU can do many sequences in parallel, a 50ms hold plus model decode still keeps you under target. The cost savings per token can be substantial; in our cost model we show up to 30-45% token cost reduction with modest batching for certain models.
[02:09] [02:09] Sarah Lee: And how does KV cache play with batching? We have many repeated prefixes (financial disclaimers, signatures) across requests.
[02:16] Jon Park (SE): Great question. Two parts: prefix caching (aka prefix or partial prompt caching) stores the KV state for repeated prefixes — so you don't re-run the prefix through the entire attention stack. KV cache operates on token-level keys/values; when hit rates are high, you avoid computing the prefix entirely and only do the suffix generation. That reduces both latency and cost. Batching still helps on the suffix. When you combine moderate batching + high KV hit rate you compound savings.
[02:39] [02:39] Carlos Rivera: Our traffic has about 35-40% exact-prefix repeats and another 20% near-duplicates (slightly different client IDs). Is that enough to see material wins?
[02:49] Jon Park (SE): Yes, 35-40% exact is very meaningful. In our example cost model I pulled up, with a 40% prefix hit and batch size of 8 on the remainder, cost per scored request drops by approx 38% vs naive single-request. We'll walk through the numbers in the spreadsheet.
[03:06] [03:06] Maya Chen: Sharing the benchmark spreadsheet link now — https://redwood.app/share/ATLAS-optimize-batch-model (note: internal link).
[03:12] [03:12] Priya Nair: I see columns for token count, base GPU tokens/sec, batch factor, cache hit rate — can you explain the assumptions?
[03:19] Jon Park (SE): Sure. Base assumptions: model TDP is 100 tokens/sec baseline for the model family on our target GPU, then we scale that by batching efficiency curve (diminishing returns after batch 16). Cache hit savings assume average prefix length of 40 tokens; if prefix is cached you only bill for the suffix tokens. We also include a small overhead for cache lookup and KV transfer — sometimes transcription shows this as K-V cash or K V cash in our logs :)
[03:40] [03:40] Sarah Lee: (laughs) We've actually seen transcriptions call it K V cash before.
[03:43] Jon Park (SE): Yeah the ASR has fun with it. Back to the model: the spreadsheet has tabs for different scenarios: hosted low-latency, hosted cost-optimized (higher batching), and dedicated with autoscale. If you look at the "Atlas baseline" tab I populated it with your numbers: 120 avg tokens, 10 req/s steady, bursts to 200 req/s during peak.
[04:02] [04:02] Carlos Rivera: Those bursts are the worry. Will caching help during peaks?
[04:06] Jon Park (SE): Caching helps reduce work per request which raises effective throughput. But one important note: caching is memory bound — KV memory usage scales with unique prefixes. In Dedicated we can give you pinned GPU memory and larger KV store to keep hit latencies low; in hosted we do eviction policies but can still get high hit rates for repetitive prefixes.
[04:24] Maya Chen: Also want to call out routing policies — Optimize recommends fallback to a cheaper model variant if we see capacity constraints. That's in the rollout plan.
[04:32] Priya Nair: How do you quantify the added complexity of managing cache invalidation when model prompts change?
[04:38] Leah Ortiz: We recommend namespacing keys by prompt template version and adding a short TTL for transient fields. If your templates change infrequently you get long-lived hits. For frequent prompt churn we surface metrics in Console to show cache hit distribution per prefix so you can decide TTL.
[04:52] [04:52] Jon Park (SE): Another real point: tokenization differences can reduce apparent hit rate. If client-side canonicalization isn't consistent, two semantically identical prefixes tokenized differently won't hit. We often avoid that by running a canonicalizer pre-send or by normalizing whitespace and punctuation at the inference edge.
[05:10] Sarah Lee: That makes sense. Can you show an example in the API flow?
[05:14] Jon Park (SE): Sure — in the Console demo: API request shows a "prefix_id" header option, or you can pass the prefix inline and Redwood will auto-detect repeated prefixes and register them in Optimize. If we detect high repeat we can suggest promoting those prefixes to persistent KV entries.
[05:31] [05:31] Carlos Rivera: Is there an SDK we run client-side to annotate prefixes?
[05:34] Maya Chen: Yes we have SDK helpers in our Java/Python SDK that compute a prefix fingerprint and optionally upload canonicalized prefix to the control plane.
[05:41] Priya Nair: Security question: uploading prefixes—does that contain PII? Our prefixes can include account IDs.
[05:47] Kevin O'Neill (Security): Right we need to make sure any prefix data that's uploaded is encrypted and stored according to our data retention policy.
[05:52] Leah Ortiz: You can opt to keep the prefix store in your VPC (Private). For hosted mode we redact certain fields by default and you can enable customer-managed KMS. We'll include the KMS flow in the security pack.
[06:02] [06:02] Maya Chen: Back to numbers: looking at the spreadsheet scenario with 40% prefix hit + batch size 8, p95 remained ~180ms in our simulated benchmark and cost per request dropped by ~38%. If you push batch to 12 you get another 8% cost savings but p95 climbs toward 260ms in that scenario.
[06:21] Priya Nair: So there's a clear tradeoff. For our product we want to keep p95 under 250ms so batch 8 looks like sweet spot.
[06:27] Jon Park (SE): Yep and Optimize can enforce runtime target — we can set adaptive batching policy that bounds hold time to keep p95 within threshold and still opportunistically batch.
[06:36] [06:36] Sarah Lee: Any impact on hallucination/quality when you do prefix caching?
[06:40] Jon Park (SE): Not directly; prefix caching just avoids re-computing prefix. The only risk is if the prefix version and model variant mismatch — that's why we tie prefix entries to model/version hashes. If you update model or template you should invalidate or re-score a sample. Optimize flags model-prefix compatibility automatically.
[06:58] [06:58] Carlos Rivera: Is there a demo of the autoscaler working with batch changes?
[07:02] Leah Ortiz: We have a recorded demo; I can link it and also we'll run a live dry-run during the pilot where we'll replay your traffic with different cache/BPS configs.
[07:10] Maya Chen: Next I'll do a quick API snippet: POST /v1/generate with headers x-redwood-prefix-id: <id> or body prefix. And cost metrics appear in Console under per-token breakdown.
[07:22] [07:22] Priya Nair: How do we set SLOs per route? We have different SLOs for fraud scoring vs enrichment requests.
[07:28] Jon Park (SE): You can set per-route latency SLOs in Console and Optimize will recommend per-route batching policies. Route-level dashboards show p50/p95/p99 and cost-in-USD per thousand requests.
[07:39] [07:39] Sarah Lee: Cool. Anything on model quantization interplay with batching and cache?
[07:44] Jon Park (SE): Quantization reduces CPU/GPU memory and speeds up token throughput which pushes the batching efficiency curve right — meaning you get more throughput gains for same batch size. But note quantization may change model quality slightly; Optimize ties quality regressions to eval sets and will alert if quantization regresses your evals.
[07:59] [07:59] Kevin O'Neill (Security): One last compliance point: we need audit logs of who accessed prefix store and when.
[08:04] Leah Ortiz: Console includes audit logs and we can forward to your SIEM; logs include prefix access events and cache evictions. We'll add retention policy options to the security pack.
[08:13] [08:13] Sarah Lee: Ok this was super helpful. Let's summarize next steps.
[08:17] Maya Chen: Recap: we will send the cost model spreadsheet and demo recording; Jon will prepare benchmark plan; customer will share anonymized traffic; security will confirm KMS/audit requirements. We'll propose pilot dates for a 2-week benchmark window.
[08:30] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Any other questions?
[08:33] Carlos Rivera: Not from infra, thanks.
[08:35] Kevin O'Neill (Security): I'll review the SOC2 + KMS docs when you send them.
[08:38] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email, I'll attach the spreadsheet and the recording and a short checklist.
[08:45] [08:45] END OF RECORDING

Notes: occasional ASR artifacts: "K V cash" for KV cache, speaker mislabels in a few segments. Recorded on Zoom. Demo assets referenced: https://redwood.app/share/ATLAS-optimize-batch-model and security pack link: https://redwood.app/sec-pack/atlas (internal).
